[i]Crypt of the NecroDancer[/i] is quietly genius.

It's exactly what you would imagine a game to be like if you were told it's a roguelike, but in real time, with the turns lasting as long as the beat of a soundtrack — because they are, in fact, set to a soundtrack. This kind of "X meets Y" high concept game (roguelike meets rhythm game, in this case) is easy to think up, but not as easy to turn into a good game, if the failed examples littering Steam are any indication. [i]NecroDancer[/i] not only works, but works [i]well[/i] — it's an astounding feat of game design, and it's likely you won't even notice that while you're playing because it just feels natural.

This is one of the few roguelikes that deserves the description "easy to pick up, hard to master", as most roguelikes are not even all that easy to pick up. [i]NecroDancer[/i] has a tutorial that lasts all of 90 seconds, and contains everything you need to get started. Getting through the first set of levels will take a little more time, but can still be done in an hour or two. But make no mistake, the difficulty ramps up over a total of four zones (each with three levels and a boss level, for a total of 16 levels). And if you think that's the end of it, you're wrong — there's a separate story mode to play through all the zones in sequence rather than separately, and to unlock all the characters (each with their own gimmicks that change the way you play) you have to complete the game multiple times. This is a true roguelike in that the peak difficulty is insane and completing the game with every character is a challenge restricted to only a handful of demigods, but it's also a true roguelike in that it's fair and rewards strategic play and perseverance. And all that to a great beat!

I haven't even completed the third zone yet and I can already tell it will be many hours more before I chip my teeth on the [i]really[/i] difficult parts, but I felt like I needed to get this review out before the current sale is over, even if my experience is incomplete. This game is almost certainly worth it at full price if you're into roguelikes, but at sale price it's a no-brainer. If it looks like anything you might like, buy it. Even if you can't make your way through it, you'll still get your money's worth for the time you're playing it.

I've played this game for last 4 months of its Early Access. It already looked very promising and awesome. With the release it took me only a few hours of playtime to confirm everything I was ready to write about.

This is a rogue-like rhythm dungeon crawler, as you've probably read on the store page. The genre is quite unique - its gameplay is a blend of turn-based combat but it's constrained by the boundaries of the "beats" of the music of the level (unlike a lot of rhythm games it's very forgiving on beat accuracy and there's a reason for that: it's quite action-packed, so when you have a few skeletons, fiery dogs and a dragon converging on you - you can't really follow the beats within 20% margin what is usual for rhythm games).

First things first: this is a rhythm game and its soundtrack wirtten by Danny Baranowsky is just pure essence of awesomeness. Randomly generated levels are extremely well done. When I say extremely I mean it. This game doesn't have unbeatable generations. It may be easier or harder, but it's a fair rogue-like, if you die - it's your fault. It's not like rogue's tale when you can be killed on first turn the moment you spawn. So you won't really be stomped by something you can't beat.

With the release the game has been augmented with some kind of plot which makes it a bit more beautiful than a rogue-like w/o a plot. Also this game even during Early Access didn't have any gamebreaking bugs. In 80h I never had a single crash or anything else that'd ruin my gaming experience, since technically this is kind of a day1 for this game - it's exremely polished, which is a good example what Early Access system should be used for and how.

With cutscenes you are being rewarded with when you complete "zones" with different characters, with easier and harder characters themselves, with a big variety of items, leaderboards, daily challenges - delivering beatdowns to the beat in this game is guaranteed to be one your best rogue-like experiences ever.

I only have two things to say about this game:
1. It is very good and Highly polished. Haven't really seen a bug affecting the gameplay in any significant way.  The pixel art and animations are pristine.  It seems clear to me that the game devs truly believe in this game and want it to succeed, which I admire.

2. It is very hard.  (Note: This is NOT a complaint, just trying to inform people before they buy, which is the whole point of reviews)  If you want to succeed and have fun, you have to put in some serious time to get good, which I understand isn't the type of thing a lot of people want when it comes to video games. (And that 's totally fine!)
It has a relatively simple premise, that you can only control it with the D-pad and move to the beat. But it still has a high skill ceiling, not unlike the old arcade games that seem to have inspired this modernized style of pixel graphics, crisp animations, and catchy soundtracks.
The game will punish your every mistake - to win (I'm talking about All Zones Mode here), you have play nearly perfectly.  Because of the way the game is designed, you have very few second chances, and getting more second chances involves sacrifices which will hurt your chances of finishing the game, each of which lasts anywhere from Less than a minute, to over half an hour.  Getting good involves learning the exact game mechanics for every enemy or object in the game, and then being to demonstrate that knowledge at a fast pace.
Yeah, in my opinion it's a Great game, but you better be up for a challenge.

This game was so good Nintendo asked the developers to make a sequel with the Zelda licence.
Buy it.

There have been plenty of rogue-like games in the last few years, but this is definitely one of the most unique and original. The concept is strangely brilliant, the art is great, and the music is awesome, so the whole package seems pretty stunning at first glance. However, when you look under the hood, it's not flawless...the concept may be amazing, but the execution is a little bit janky at times. There are times when I know that I'm 100% on the beat, and yet the game simply isn't registering that I'm on target, leading to my untimely death. I'm a musician, so I have a good sense of rhythm and timing - something seemed off here. There's just not enough precision to the mechanics, which can really sink you when you're facing a boss or going up against a  big room filled with tough enemies. There are definitely a few frustrations that you'll have to deal with to get into a groove here. I would defintely still recommend this, despite  whatever shortcomings it may have, because the idea is great and the development team has gotten pretty dang close to nailing it. There's also the ability to add in your own music, which is a fantastic feature...I pumped in some Tribe Called Quest, Wu-Tang, Biggie, etc., and then the game was really bumping and twice as fun. Get this on sale and it'll be money well-spent, as long as you recognize that there's gonna be a serious learning curve when it comes to getting into the game's idea of rhythm.

Every enemy (except bats) moves in a predefined pattern that triggers on the beat of the songs (which are all super catchy btw). So you KNOW what they're going to do, and when you inevitably die you'll find yourself saying "man I know I can do that right next time". Beating all four worlds back to back with Cadence (nowhere close to the hardest achievement) is one of my proudest moments.
Move, cast, and attack with the beat as you delve deeper towards the crypt of the Necrodancer. With great replayability and a sweet soundtrack, it's a must play in my books.

Huge respect.

As a fan of both rhythm games and dungeon crawlers, I find Crypt of the NecroDancer as quite the diamond in the rough.  The rhythm component adds a dimension of gameplay that I find captivating.  It helps that the soundtrack rocks even if it is a bit synth-ey.

* Replayability.  LOTS of replayability.

[h1]The good[/h1]
+Amazing gameplay concept: a real-time combat dungeon crawler ruled by music beats
+Superb soundtrack. Danny Baranowsky produces yet another gem - you might find yourself head bobbing 
+Great artistic direction - all monsters are easily identifiable, readable, and just plain nice to look at. Bosses' designs are musical themed, which is a nice touch

A finely crafted rhythm-based dungeon crawler with great soundtrack, uncommon gameplay and good challenge and replay value

Crypt of the NecroDancer is a roguelike rhythm game, developed by Brace Yourself Games. Releasing in April 2015 on Steam and then later released on PS4 and Vita in February 2016. 

NecroDancer is a really unique gaming experience. Every action you take must be in line with the beat of the soundtrack. This includes moving and attacking the enemies. The reward for hitting the beat each time is getting a higher coin multiplier, failing to hit the beat resets your multiplier. Not hitting the beat does not deal any damage to your character, it is just a pain as sometimes your multiplier can often be the thing between successfully completing a level and not. There are a handful of different enemies in the game, which you can learn their pattern of movements if you pay close attention. They all have a predefined path which you should learn to do damage to them or avoid them completely. 

Throughout the dungeons, you will find loot; these can be weapons, armour, and useable items such as bombs or potions. The coins you earn can also be used in the dungeon’s shops to let you purchase upgrades on the fly.  The game also has a central hub; this is where you can purchase upgrades that will stay active throughout your play through, such as unlocking an extra chest to spawn on each level for example. One of the ways in which the game forces you to keep moving, is the hidden time limit on each level. Once the song ends you will be forced to move onto the next zone, which may result in you missing out on the reward of more coins or upgrades. I think this is a nice addition as it stops people from using a slow and methodical method and force you to keep up with the tempo and beat of the song. 

Graphically, NecroDancer uses the 8bit pixel theme very well. It looks really pretty and very vibrant with colours the majority of the time. The UI is clean and clear with all of the relevant information, especially the Heartbeat sensor at the bottom, which after an hour or two, you won’t need to pay any attention to as you will be so in tune with the soundtracks that you can move on your own. Of course a game that revolves around rhythm needs a half decent soundtrack, NecroDancer certainly delivers there thankfully. With some original music composed by Danny Baranowsky.

As with most roguelike games, the more you play the easier they get. Since NecroDancer requires more skill than anything else, this is more so the case than ever before. Once you get the beat down, you can conquer pretty much anything the game throws at you. Throw in a few permanent upgrades and you really won’t have any problems. The game has a handful of really unique boss fights too. The end one is probably the most memorable of them all though as it adds some very unique game play mechanics in which I thoroughly enjoyed. 

All of the levels and stages across the game are randomly generated, so you will never run into the same dungeon layout twice. This of course adds to the replay ability of the game already; but NecroDancer doesn’t stop there. In the main game hub, you will also have access to a daily challenge, in which every player who plays the challenge will face the same map, and your aim is to get the best score possible at the end. This definitely makes the game have plenty of longevity and gives you a reason to load the game up every few days to take part in this daily event even after finishing the story mode.  The main story took me seven hours to complete which I think is a decent amount of time; where you will get the most content is from re-running the stages unlocking new characters, playing the daily challenges and working your way up the leader boards. 

I really wanted to play the game using a controller, but I couldn’t get my 360 pad to work sadly. Whilst the keyboard controls are fine, I feel the controller would have been that little bit better to use. Everything else works as intended in the game. A neat little feature is that you can import your own music collection to the game too, having you match the beat of your favourite tunes! 

Crypt of the NecroDancer is an absolute god send a roguelike game. The originality of the gameplay is something which every other developer should take note of. The gorgeous pixel graphics art style is really well done too. This game just screams of character and pure fun. I cannot recommend this game enough for roguelike fans, and fans of the indie scene. I urge everyone to pick this game up for the low price of £10,99. It will not disappoint.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is absolutely fantastic, and a no-brainer to pick up when it's on sale (Steam Summer Sale, 80% off at $2.99).  Even still, at the regular price this game is definitely worth picking up.

[h1]What is Necrodancer?[/h1]

Crypt of the Necrodancer is an old-school Zelda style dungeon crawler (think, A Link to the Past) that requires the player to take on challenging dungeons and bosses to progress through the game.  What sets it apart from any other games is its use of a music/rhythm mechanic for movement; you can only move one "block" of space at a time along with the beat of the games soundtrack (or your own music, if you want to use a custom soundtrack!).  Moving constantly with the beat and not taking damage from enemies builds your gold multiplier, allowing you to get more gold for character upgrades, items, and weapons to use through your run.  Stop moving to the beat, make a wrong move (i.e. jumping into a wall/trap) or take a hit, and your multiplier resets.  Does the rhythm movement mechanic seem gimmicky?  Not to worry, it's incredibly fun and the phenominal soundtrack makes for a great experience.  Custom soundtrack options are also great; the auto-beat-importer works very well, and if necessary you can create custom beats for any songs you import.

[h1]Combat and Weapons[/h1]

Combat in Necrodancer is fast and incredibly fun.  There's no "attack wildly and pray for success" here; successful combat requires deliberate and calculated attacks/movement.  In addition to the fun beat mechanic, weapon variability is what makes Necrodancer so fun and engaging.  Weapons vary greatly in attack types, range, buffs (i.e. knockback, freezing, etc.), and strength.  Certain weapons will definitely be more successful against some enemies than others, and your preference will largely depend on the play style you prefer.

In addition to combat, the other two mechanics you'll consider are digging (via your shovel) and vision.  A large part of dungeons is finding your way around, digging up "diamonds" to use for permanent upgrades and other unlockables, and finding hidden rooms for temporary items or character buffs.  Both your shovel and vision (view distance) can be upgraded to allow more efficient exploration and finding better items for your runs.

Runs last until you complete the dungeon and move on to the next, die, or the level's song ends (~5 minutes) and kicks you to the next level of the dungeon automatically (but, if you dont find the exit and the level auto-ends, you lose your score multiplier).

[h1]Progression[/h1]

Progression in Necrodancer is very difficult, but fair and rewards mastering the movement/beat mechanic.  Learning enemy and boss attack patters is paramount to success, and enemies very greatly from level to level and present a great challenge as you progress. 

Each time you die you are returned to a lobby where you can buy upgrades for your character to improve for your next run.  You can only spend "diamonds" in the lobby earned from your immediate previous run, and starting a new one resets all of your "diamonds" that can be spent in the lobby.  With a variety of dungeons, bosses and increasing difficulty as you progress you'll definitely get some good (and fun) play time out of this game.  There are also a large variety of different playable characters that change game mechanics and add tons of play time and very high replay value.  For example, the "Bard" can move freely (is unlocked from the beat mechanic), but every time you move functions as a "beat" in the game - so as you move, enemies move, and the faster you move, the faster they move, and the faster you move, the faster the timer for the level expires still requiring you to be deliberate in movement.

[b]Verdict: Absolutely recommend, 8/10[/b], one of the best casual, low-commitment games I've played in a very, very long time.

I don't like this game. But frankly, that's on me. The central mechanic just never clicked, and I didn't want to put in the effort to force it. I don't want to leave a negative review because of my own indifference to what is clearly a good game, so Instead, this.

Before you buy it, remember one thing: this game is hard. This game is hard. THIS GAME IS HARD. In particular, there's a skill barrier on level 2 (or 3, if you luckily go through 2 once), another skill barrrier on the final boss, even harder skill barrier on the final boss in DLC and a super-duper-hard skill barrier on Aria (I couldn't break through the last one no matter how hard I tried).

If you are not afraid of challenges, this game is for you :).

The game is exactly what you see in promo videos - a rhytm-based dungeon crawler. Music is really nice and monsters are very creative, making game's climate really cool. Many barriers mentioned in the beginning are connected to learning monsters' patterns - they are (in most cases) deterministic, but sometimes hard to follow under time's pressure. Especially in boss fights, when you may have around 10 monsters on the field and only half a second to decide where you move. The one thing you learn through this game is to play with cold mind, because mistakes tend to escalate quickly.

Story is not bad - it's limited to short cutscenes between levels, but keep everything together, giving some reasoning to our actions and to play other characters. And I liked authors' humor ;).

I really had fun playing and taking challenges, game devs made so many of them that achieving everything takes loooooooong hours. Probably you'll never be even close to get all the achievements. But if you really like playing with rhytm and you're stubborn enough to get through even hard challenges, I strongly recommend this game :).

I made it to zone 4, and there I realised that fighting enemies felt like a chore rather than fun. I get that you're supposed to "dance" with the enemies, but I dunno.... it just felt tedious going through their patterns and slowly whittling them down. I greatly enjoy both rhythm and roguelike games, and the overwhelmingly positive reviews made me believe I was gonna love this, but now I feel that this game does justice to neither of those genres. 

In particular, the roguelike part feels extremely lacking in the sense of exploration and mystery, and the rhythm part is reduced to simply pressing buttons to the beat, all the time, without any  variation. As other reviewers have pointed out, this game is more like speed-chess with pieces you have to figure out on the fly. I could go to the practice rooms and grind to memorize the enemy patterns, but where's the fun in that? I've also read the suggestion to play as the Bard, but then there's no point in playing this game... I could play other, more dedicated roguelikes.

It's nice to see the developers still working to improve the game, so I'll throw some suggestions out there. I think there needs to be more animations for telegraphing when an enemy is going to attack. A lot of enemies do have such animations, so it's annoying to see others without them (the skeletons with the shields and bats, for instance).  Also, it would be really nice to have an in-game journal/bestiary so I can read up on enemies and items I have encountered, with animations showing how an enemy moves/attacks. It's really tedious to go to practice rooms and actually fight an enemy to figure out its patterns.

I am not completely against this game... I can see why a lot of people love it, and I might even come back and try it again some time. But currently I am just not having fun.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is a timeless masterpiece of an Indie game that never seems to bore me. I have bought this game on 3 separate platforms, and I don't believe that I wasted a single bit of time spent in it.

Crypt is a very interesting and fun fusion of both rhythm and puzzle, while presenting itself as a dungeon-crawler. The controls are simple, but the skill ceiling is so insanely high for something so surface-level in appearance. Missing a button press on a note resets a stacking "Coin Multiplier" which rewards you for treating this game with precision, taking damage also does this. There is no such thing as "Mandatory Damage" in this game, you are perfectly able to control yourself in order to avoid haphazard conditions, and every single enemy has a pattern or "Tell" that indicates their movements, attack patterns, and the sort. 

If that wasn't enough, Necrodancer also provides endless replayability in the form of achievements, unlockables, speedrunning, daily challenges, and different gameplay based on character choice. There is even a "Dungeon Maker", and an active Modding community. You can import your own music, change the soundtracks based on around 12 different artists, and plop premade skins (And skins you make via modding) onto player characters. 

I spent around 60 bonus hours on the Switch port and around 40 on the Playstation 4 version, and I can say that this game holds up extremely well and runs extremely well on all platforms. All versions of this game have a minor issue where the game might crash during startup, or you might have to rarely recalibrate the timing of songs and visuals. The switch port is definitely the weakest of all, but this game has love and effort put into every single port. I would definitely advise getting the Steam Vers. since the community workshop adds so much to your enjoyment of the game.
Perfect Example: There's a character you unlock at the end of the story arc named "Aria." She dies in one hit, can't miss a note, and is stuck with a dagger. If you get preoccupied or have to pause the game in the middle of an area, that can be completely fatal. A mod I love is the "Transparent Menu" mod which allows you to see the beat indicator while the game is paused. I just can't use it on Switch or PS4.


On another mark, I do believe the writing for this game is genuinely hilarious and fun. There are some weak parts, like the cutscene at the start of Aria's arc, but I have a soft spot for music puns... The entire game is music puns. Every character has some sort of reference to music in their name/appearance, every enemy has a name in the credits that associates with an element of music, all the bosses are clever references to genres and/or dumb puns, etc. I absolutely adore the tone this game has - Serious but fun.

The DLC adds a lot, and I appreciate everything it brought to the table. I do wish zone 5 was optional, especially when playing as Aria, but I still adore it. (Doing all zones mode - dlc still leaves the DLC area in the game...) But with all the added content and quality of life changes that have been listed for Amplified, I'm ok with it not being toggleable.
//Note: The Danganronpa sountrack add-on doesn't have songs for Amplified :(//

Flaws? Yeah, there are a few, but they're so indescribably worthless that it barely bothers me, the Switch port having the majority of flaw. (There was a bug that required me to uninstall the game after beating the game as Cadence...)
Installing too many mods might occasionally crash your game, messing with full-screen/windowed mode might crash the game, and there is no borderless fullscreen mode. Mods that worked without DLC don't work and/or aren't compatable with DLC. That's literally all for the negatives, really.

You might originally think the game isn't registering your movements, but you need to actually follow the rythm. If you still think that your button inputs don't match with the song, try re-calibrating in the menu.
Having issues with learning new enemies? Toggle hearts in the menu.
Want to see more of the map? Mess with the view multiplier.
Want to practice CBT? Play Monk.
Want to take Speed? Play Bolt.
Never wanna die? Play Nocturna.
Want to confuse yourself? Play the repainted mod.

This game is one of those where, now that I get a chance to dive into it, I wish I had done so much, much sooner.  I've played so very, very many roguelikes/lites/whatevers over the years, and of course many games in a general sense.  This, honestly, may be one of the greatest of all of them, which isnt exactly something I say lightly.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is two things:  A turn-based roguelike, and a rhythm game.  The core mechanic is that the "turns" pass with the rhythm of the song being played.  On each beat, you make a move, and enemies also make a move.  This creates a game that is actually very fast-moving and active.  You must constantly be doing stuff, as if you skip a beat, or if you screw up the timing on one, Bad Things will tend to happen (depending on who you're playing as).  For most characters this involves your coin multiplier dropping to nothing (which can cause any Obsidian equipment to become weak), and maybe certain items might vanish.  For a couple of others, they just outright die if you screw up even once.  The rhythm mechanic is the absolute core of everything in the game.  Not only do all of the game's mechanics and design aspects revolve around it, but it's also a huge part of what makes the game so very, very fun. Two genres that appear to make no sense together are fused regardless, and the result is just stunning.

The good thing is, you dont have to be a master at music games to play this.  Necrodancer doesnt require the hyper-exact timing that most rhythm games do.  Dont get me wrong, it's still easy to screw up, but this is a game that anyone can get into.  Even the way the rhythm works... with many music games it's this chaotic pile of interspersed notes flying at you in various patterns along with the music.  In Necrodancer, it's an extremely steady beat. It's displayed at the bottom of the screen constantly, but almost immediately you'll find that you dont have to look at it.

However, that doesnt mean it isnt tough to deal with in other ways. One huge aspect that goes along with this is the fact that you MUST make some sort of movement on every beat.  You cannot simply stand still; that'll cause the aforementioned Bad Things to happen.  So you must either move, use an item, use a spell, or dig at a wall, on every single beat.  This constant forced action goes along well with the whole dancing theme of the game, but also adds alot to the challenge.  It can be difficult to place yourself into the right position to deal with the myriad foes that will attack you from all angles.  It does create a high learning curve... at first you're going to die over and over and over again simply due to this aspect, which could mean frustration.  But once you get used to it, it just WORKS.  

Not that it'll ever get easy, mind you.  The game's difficulty ranges from "difficult" to "completely absurd".  Much of this has to do with not only the core mechanic, but the enemies you'll face.  Every floor is absolutely stuffed with monsters.  And these monsters arent the ultra-simple traditional sorts that simply walk at you and deal damage.  Every individual monster type has a unique pattern and special abilities, and learning those behaviors and traits is the most important thing when it comes to your survival.  Some enemies are simple:  skeletons for instance only move every other beat, and they raise their arms up on the beat before they do move. Easy to understand.   Others are much more confusing to deal with.  The infamous Red Dragon for instance has the ability to fire a blazing deathray to the left or right; it'll always try to do this if you are on the same horizontal line as it is, and you get exactly one beat to get out of the way of this extremely damaging attack.  Skeletons may not be so bad, but that dragon is the bane of many players and requires great care and special techniques to defeat.  The good thing is, enemy behavior is very easily understood, very well telegraphed, and NOT stuffed with RNG (with certain exceptions, but even those can be understood in a way), yet these facts absolutely do not detract from the challenge they produce.

Fortunately you have all sorts of different weapons and items to use.  The game's combat system is fantastic, and one of the reason for it is the weapons.  Each weapon has a "hit pattern" where it can damage tiles in front of you.  The basic dagger only damages the tile directly in front of you as you attack.  A longsword however can hit two tiles away.   A whip on the other hand has that very short range, but also a huge straight spread to the side.  Every single weapon type is useful in some way, and every weapon type comes in a variety of interesting flavors, as do other types of equipment.  For example, obsidian items base their power on your coin multiplier.  Blood items do things with your health.  Glass items are very strong but shatter if you get hit.  There are many item categories, including shovels that let you dig at walls, and torches that not only increase vision range but let you see THROUGH walls, making "hidden" rooms a major aspect of the game.   The items in the game are all sorts of fun to use, whether they're equipment or spells or whatever.  They are very, very well thought out and usually easy to understand.

However, the game isnt always so easy to grasp.  Shrines for instance can be very confusing in terms of exactly how they work.  Many times you'll run into a new one, try it out, go "WTF?" and then die horribly, not because the effect was bad, but because you had no clue what to do with it.  Other quirky mechanics like hidden shops, or the extremely varied effects of each different character (and there are MANY characters) can take awhile to really get the hang of.  There is alot of depth here, but that also means alot to learn.  This is NOT an easy game, and chances are, it's going to take you quite some time to beat it even once.  But it has features to help you learn... lots of such features, actually, something hardly any roguelikes ever do.  It makes it easy to practice against specific foes or test things out.  It even has a full level editor and Steam Workshop support.  There is so very, very much going on here (and even more if you get the fantastic DLC).

Overall, it's a very difficult game (and the difficulty just keeps going higher, and higher, and higher, as you continue to play it), yet one with neverending replay value, and one that I honestly just never get tired of. It also has the very, very rare quality of doing everything it can to help you learn in a non-frustrating way (heck, one particular character turns it into a TRULY turn-based game, letting you experiment and learn without having to worry about the rhythm, and he's unlocked from the start).  It's just plain FUN in a way that very few games truly manage, with a level of quality that is also rarely seen.  Every single aspect of it ties together to create something truly amazing.  Even if you have a hard time with it at first, stick with it:  It's absolutely worth dealing with that brutal learning curve.  This is something you dont want to miss.  I've reviewed many games on here... but this outdoes nearly all of them.  It's that good, in my opinion.  

Oh, and did I mention that the soundtrack is absolutely incredible?  You can use your own songs, too.  Good things, in a game where the rhythm is everything.

This is likely my favorite game of all time.  It combines brilliant music, good pixel art and highly difficult roguelike elements with the unique challenge of rhythm games.  Runs can be short enough to race with friends, and the online racing community is a fantastic group of people (races are organized external to the game - sadly there is no online multiplayer).

The game provides a variety of items so from one run to the next you will often end up with an entirely different build, and it takes a lot of time to get practiced with every build.  There is also the challenge of playing low%, taking no items at all and trying to clear that way.

The game provides some challenges that can take thousands of hours to have a good chance at completing - unlocking Coda is one enormous milestone (which I only recently passed) and beating a run with her is an even more difficult feat.  That said, the difficulty is rarely the game giving you impossible situations, but instead very difficult ones that test your ability.  I almost always look back after I die and realize the mistake that cost me that run, be it a silly decision or a matter of reaction time.

The DLC adds 4 new characters and some new modes which are generally fun but sometimes not as balanced as the standard All Zones Mode.  It also adds a new zone with new enemies, and many new items.  The changes made by the DLC do a good job addressing some of the balance issues with the base game, but the DLC also adds some items that are arguably quite overpowered.

The game is quite easy to mod if you are interested in changing the gameplay, either by altering enemies, items, or any aspect of the graphics.  Hopefully in the near future we get access to the source code for more modding power.

This one is certainly a bang for your buck.
The idea behind the gameplay is simple. It won't take long to get the hang of the rhythm element, and needing to dance around each enemy's predictable pattern is punishing but fair, and very fun.

The difficulty is highly adjustable, with one character allowing you to completely ignore the rhythm, moving at your own pace, and plenty of characters that increase the difficulty to the point where the challenge can be as great as you could possibly wish.

I personally have only scraped the surface of this game, but would still highly recommend it to those who want a challenging roguelike (seriously the game is just Rogue but if it was good and a rhythm game). with a banger OST.

And if it's of interest, you can play this game with one hand, as it only uses the arrow keys, which is nice.

I've always been a fan of games that utilize rhythm not as a concept, but as a mechanic. Think of Patapons, a game that's about army management, yet it has that charm thanks to the mechanic of having to give commands by playing out specific rhythms.

In the same vein, Necrodancer is your standard roguelike, but with the element of having to perform all actions to the rhythm, and thanks to the game's design, humour and balancing, it has that charm you can't find elsewhere. But at the same time, it stays immensely challenging; having to solve logic puzzles while having very little time to react turn-to-turn makes the gameplay extremely fast paced and strategic.

At its core, the game is not supposed to be easy. Not in the slightest. But it is well aware of that, and it grants the player the power to improve at their own leisure. You can't even play all zones mode from the very start, you first have to beat the individual zones, and you are given very generous bonuses doing so to make sure you aren't overwhelmed. The game also introduces training modes and even ability to start runs with items a la assist mode.

To beat the game you just have to beat all 4 zones individually with the three story characters: Cadence, Melody and Aria. While the first 2 are pretty straightforward to deal with after enough experience, Aria is the true final test of the game, requiring you to essentially master it. I won't spoil what the characters do nor what the story is, as I found it very intruiging to learn by myself.

After you beat these characters, you've essentially beaten the game. You've seen the story and you conquered one of the hardest characters in the game. But from the achievement and content perspective, you still have a lot to do. And climbing that mountain of feats is a never ending cliff that just keeps getting steeper and steeper. Let me explain:

In total, including the story characters, there are 9 characters, each with their own quirks that make them play out much more differently from one another. For instance, Eli doesn't have a weapon but an infinite supply of bombs which he can throw at enemies, Dorian moves two spaces at once, Dove has to play the game pacifist style. Majority of the characters are fun on their own, but some other ones pose a huge challenge, testing your skills in different areas.

Aside from Aria, other challenging characters are Monk and Bolt. Monk has vow of poverty, which means picking up any gold will kill him instantly. Since every enemy drops gold, this turns the character into a huge test when it comes to kiting and managing the minefield that will inevitably emerge when clearing rooms. Bolt is probably the craziest character, and has to play the game at double speed. This makes the character extremely fast paced and requires a significantly more strategic approach, as reacting to situations at such speed is simply not humanly possible, and that's when you know how to keep the tempo - which is extremely daunting in itself. On this character, the slowest song is already faster than the fastest song on any different character, which goes to show how insane it gets.

Additionally, the game has an 'all characters run' which requires you to beat all zones mode with all 9 characters in a row. If you die once, you have to start the streak from zero, and items dont transfer between runs. This run requires absolute mastery over each character, and thus the game itself. But completing it will unlock the 10th character, not included in all chars run, which is so absurd not even the lead designer could beat the game with it - he gave up after completing the first zone. That character is Coda.

Coda is probably the most ridiculous challenge to exist in any game, and as someone who does enjoy challenging themselves and achieved a few feats in various genres, this character trumps everything I've ever done in terms of absurdity and tenacity required for completion. Like every other character, to unlock the respective achievement, you need to clear all zones mode with Coda. But now, let me say what the character actually is: it's a combination of Aria, Monk and Bolt, combined into one character. Full list of mechanics is:

- you can only use the default dagger as a weapon
- you are stuck at half a heart, meaning any hit will kill you instantly
- missing any beat will kill you
- all enemies drop gold, and picking up gold kills you instantly
- game plays at double speed

Even on paper this sounds absolutely ridiculous. The combination of double speed and missing beats killing you is already insane enough, and combine it with other downsides. This character requires insane amount of commitment, requiring you to essentially learn the game inside out and truly perfect all the skills required to even have a CHANCE at clearing the character. The whole run takes around 10 minutes, but commitment on the character alone requires well over 200 hours if you're up to the challenge, and that's after all the skill buildup you had to go through to unlock the character in this place.

Is it absurd? Yes. But is it impossible? Probably not.

But so is everything in life until you've done it enough. When I first unlocked coda I thought I would play it as a joke at most, but as I kept putting time in I saw real improvement, and now so much time has passed I am finally standing up to the task and am on my way to clear the character. At times it feels impossible, ridiculous, something I would never do, something others have done probably because they aren't human, but as I keep going I know I will eventually stand triumphant and conquer this ridiculous challenge.

But back on track: The game in itself is awesome. It's plain fun, soundtrack is awesome and, as I mentioned, it's an absurdly difficult climb that only the most dedicated people will conquer. Regardless if you're here to have a nice casual experience or truly stress test your human abilities, this game is a no brainer. If it even slightly tickles you fancy, buy it.

TLDR:
For casuals, it's probably one of the most well balanced and fun roguelike experiences out there to experience.
For completionists, you better make this game your second life and consume your soul; otherwise forget completing it.

The reason why I don't recommend this game is because of the absurd and arbitrary roller coaster of a difficulty curve that this game is.

[list]
[*]Playing Cadence was a fun and invigorating challenge. I banged my head a bit trying to beat the boss, but was able to eventually overcome it. The difficulty curve was fair and steady.
[*]Playing Melody was easy - a cakewalk compared to Cadence. I beat all 4 zones in 1-2 tries, no sweat. The difficulty curve was abnormally low here, especially after beating the 4th zone with Cadence.
[*]Then we have Aria... never have I played a videogame that it so unforgiving and punishing.
[/list]

There are several major disagreements I have with this:

[list]
[*]The cliff-like difficulty spike: especially going from Melody to Aria, this was a stark negative experience for me.
[*]That this ridiculous difficulty spike is included in the main storyline: This effectively locks out everyone but hardcore players from even the base storyline (Yes I'm saying that if you clear all Aria's zones I consider you a hardcore player!). Okay, so first of all I will say that this is one of my favourite games in general, but I can also clearly see that it's not for everyone. That said, let's get right into it.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is an amazing game, concept-wise. It's a mix of two genres, roguelikes and rythm games. You know it's gonna be good if it's a genre mix. Especially when it's a roguelike. And a rythm game. How awesome is that? The rythm element is omnipresent and very important, but at the same time very simple. Basically it is a dungeon crawler but with a twist - you need to perform every action to the beat! The beat is steady but gets slightly faster with your progression. Enemies and environment all act along the beat, too. You need to keep up or else they'll quickly destroy you.


Game consists of zones, each zone having 3 levels and boss chamber. There are 4 zones (Amplified DLC adds 5th zone). Every zone is differently themed, zone 3 for example revolves around elements of ice and fire (one could say it's a pretty cool zone, lit even). You can play the zones individually, slowly gather diamonds and use them to unlock new items that will help you on your way. But this is just a training. For the real roguelike feel you need to play All Zones Mode, in which you start in zone 1 and go all the way to the final boss.

Now about the story. The story is quite interesting, in my opinion. 3 of the characters (4 in DLC) are "story characters" and you need to play as them in order to witness all cutscenes and progress the story. 

There are 10 characters in total (14 with Amplified DLC), two of them are unlocked by default. Characters have unique traits and quirks, in some cases this is a major difference. Most of them just serve as an alternative challenges, for example Dove is a pacifist and cannot kill enemies (boss fights are skipped). My absolute favourite is Aria. She's locked down to 0,5 HP, can only use default dagger and dies instantly if you miss a beat. Pretty tough.

Now, regarding difficulty... Some characters are tough as fuck. I still haven't beaten Coda and I am very far from doing that. But this is all optional, really. Well, kind of. See, there's a huge difficulty spike when it comes to story. First two characters are among the easiest. But then you unlock Aria and are supposed to play as her. Most people just give up at this point. There are many characters of various in-between difficulty, but if you want to progress (and finish) the story then you need to play as Aria. 

Music. This game is all about music, isn't it? Sountrack is great. Do you know what is greater, though? The fact that there are 8 soundtracks to choose from! Each soundtrack is tied to a character, but you are free to switch them as you wish. For example, there's a metal soundtrack by Family Jules, quite fitting for Aria. Other soundtracks are: Danny Baranowsky, A_Rival, Virt, Girlfriend Records, Chipzel, Overclocked Remix and also Danganronpa.

Nice things
+ Great rythm mechanic
+ Amazing soundtracks to choose from
+ Active speedrunnin/scorerunning community
+ There's DLC that adds tons of content
+ Various characters
+ Countless musical puns

Wack things:
- Huge difficulty spike in story progression
- Countless musical puns

Easily one of the best roguelikes I've played. Having to play to the beat adds a significant but fun challenge. I'm not a big fan of electronic music like this, but this soundtrack is incredible, especially the boss pieces. 

Highly recommended, even for people like me who don't usually get into roguelikes.

Hi there, I'm here to gatekeep Crypt of the Necrodancer.

After obtaining 31 out of the game's 61 achievements, with several characters left to beat and multiple major challenges ahead mocking me like Sisyphus's boulder, I've come to some important thoughts regarding this game and its ability to keep people playing it in the first place. Although I find the game greatly enjoyable, I will outline 3 major points for why this game may turn off most players from even beating the first part of the story. 

1. Necrodancer feels like an old roguelite with some newer coats of paint

If you've played other rogue-like/lites, playing Necrodancer for a few hours will make you immediately aware that the game is essentially the last of the "old" rogue-lites like the first Binding of Isaac, Spleunky, and Rogue Legacy. While these other games have received sequels that built upon their initial mechanics, Necrodancer has been steadily added to over the years with some spinoffs like Cadence of Hyrule and the upcoming Rift of the Necrodancer. Notably, Necrodancer's story, random map generation, and interlocking systems pale in comparison to newer roguelites like Hades or Enter the Gungeon, despite a veneer of meta-progression that has become the standard for today's roguelites. 

Contributing to this feeling is the rather bland aesthetic and atmosphere of Necrodancer. Even games released around the same time like Binding of Isaac and FTL are iconic for their grimy and isolated atmospheres respectively, but Necrodancer has what is initially a generic fantasy art style that transitioned to something more anime inspired over the course of 2 DLCs (now Hatsune Miku is even in the game). Noticeable consequences of Necrodancer's inconsistent and blander art style is the contrast between character art of the original set of characters and newer DLCs, the re-skinning of Cadence's character model for all of the characters, and the clutter of different modes and training rooms on the game's main menu.

2. Necrodancer's gameplay is as wide as a puddle, but as deep as the Mariana trench

Necrodancer's rhythm mechanic is so important, that if you remove it (as the character Bard and "no beat mode" do), the game becomes a very stripped down turn-based dungeon crawler, ironically becoming closer to its progenitor rogue-like games than the many other rogue-lites that followed it. By putting a time-limit on each "turn" of a classic roguelike by setting it to a beat, Necrodancer has turned what would otherwise be a simple game into one with an extremely high mechanical skill ceiling. Luckily for Necrodancer, this is the last time Danny Baranowsky composed a worthwhile soundtrack for a game, so the songs (and multiple guest remix soundtracks!) don't let the rhythm mechanics get old. 

So, where exactly does all the mechanical skill come from beyond staying on-beat? For Necrodancer, this is from a mix of recognizing enemy patterns, the difficulty of numerous characters, and the superhuman endurance needed for many of the game's later challenges and achievements. Enemy movements and attack patterns are the main "knowledge" component of getting better at Necrodancer, which is made difficult by the lack of telegraphing for many enemy attacks (You have a single beat to react to a red dragon's infinite range fireball!) and the randomness element of throwing a dozen of these fuckers in a cramped room while trying to stay on tempo. Its as if the spirit of Terrence Fletcher from Whiplash has come to throw a virtual chair at you for being out of tune with the single black skeleton that just took 2 out of your 3 starting hearts on the first floor of the dungeon. 

3. Necrodancer has a Calvinist approach to player retention. You were either pre-selected to enjoy this game, or are guaranteed to go to hell.

Taking one look at the Necrodancer global achievements has made most people realize something is pretty fucked up about how this game designs its main set of challenges. There is a completion rate of ~45% to 8% for beating the game with the STARTING CHARACTER (Zones 1-4) and most other achievements hover around 1% or less, with the achievement for actually completing the main story (Aria All-Zones) being 0.6%. What the hell went wrong along the way that made the majority of players not even beat the game with Cadence? Is Necrodancer just the Steam equivalent of a DDR machine where you have the average person playing 3 songs and leaving or the Asian college kid grinding out full clears on the highest difficulty? 

I'm not sure if the game changed gears when it was being developed through early access or what, but the overall escalation in difficulty from Cadence to Aria (and several of the unlockable side characters) is pretty absurd. You go from Cadence, with no unique abilities, to Melody, with a unique weapon you have to use, and finally Aria, who expects you to beat each zone (12 or 15 total levels) in reverse with the worst weapon in the game without missing a beat or getting hit (Dont worry, you get an item that lets you make only one of these mistakes for the whole run). To put this shit into perspective, the average rhythm game dares you to full clear a 2-5 minute song to say you truly mastered it on your selected difficulty. Necrodancer asks you to full clear the entire soundtrack in one go if you even want to see the ending of the story. Its no wonder that this game is played by a stable population of a few hundred dedicated challenge grinders, and a transient population of people getting scared off by the high skill floor required to succeed.

4. Conclusion
Knowing myself, I'll keep grinding this game for many hours to come, as the rhythm mechanics and challenge are incredibly fun for me. But if this level of difficulty doesn't appeal to you, then your 15+ dollars are probably better spent on other roguelikes with more respect for the time needed to beat them. I haven't even mentioned the characters that make you re-learn entire mechanics like needing to avoid gold (Monk), playing the game at double tempo (Bolt), or doing both of those things at the same time while being locked to the shittiest weapon and not missing a beat (Coda, the ultimate challenge and "fuck you" by the developers). Lets not even get to achievements that want you to finish the game with all characters in a row, or one character 10 times in a row. Needless to say, Necrodancer asks of its players more than any other game I've seen to say they've 100%'d it or mastered its mechanics. If you can handle that and dont just want to refund this game before the 2 hour refund window, start rolling that boulder up the hill.

This is the most impressive rogue-like I have ever played.  CoND beautifully integrates tile based combat with music.  Each turn lasts for a beat of the current level's song, leading to fun, fast paced action.  Even during early access it felt like a complete game, and the full release is a masterpiece.

The controls are easy and straighforward, requiring only the arrow keys to play.  The graphics are simple but well made.  

The music is great.  The soundtrack was composed by Danny B, and each song is edited masterfully into the game.  CoND lets you use your own music for the levels, but I have never done it because I love the core soundtrack so much.  Despite hearing the songs hundreds of times, I never get tired of them.

The various weapons and equipment provide a wide variety of play styles and item interactions.  The enemies are well designed, each with varying movement and attack mechanics.  The boss fights are unique and wonderful experiences.  Each one is musically themed, and the varying musical styles reinforces the awesomeness of the game's music.

There is a very large amount of content and replayability.  Between items, enemies, and floor layouts, there is a lot of variation between runs.  There are high score and fastest time leaderboards which are very competitive, and people frequently race the game live.  CoND can be very difficult at first because you have to learn each weapon's mechanics and each enemy's attack patterns, but there are many tutorial and training mechanisms built into the game.  Practicing is well worth the time, and mastering the game is very rewarding.

I recommend this game to anyone.  It is an absolute must play if you like rogue-likes or music based games.

This is basically everything I want in a roguelike and it has an interesting premise: a dungeon-crawler that plays like a rhythm game. You move in time with the beat of the background music (the timing window being [b]very[/b] generous), effectively playing like a turn-based tactics game that forces each turn to be a fraction of a second. Thankfully, the music is spectacular. It's a rare instance when I fell in love with the soundtrack before I even knew it was for a game. Especially amazing is that each of the many characters has their own unique soundtrack remix, and it will even let you customize the music you want to play in each stage. 
The game's difficulty works at just the right level for basically all but the lowest level of players, and that skill ceiling is very high. Unlike some other roguelikes that require you to get lucky to progress well, this game is very fair, so when I lose, I can usually identify exactly where I made bad decisions. Most enemies have a set pattern on how they work (the ones that move randomly are rather inconsequential). If you can identify the pattern and can think quickly, you can manage even the most chaotic of situations. Completionists beware: this game is a nightmare to 100% complete, and I love it for that. The number of modes and characters here are huge, each providing extra challenge and/or play styles to help keep the game from becoming monotonous. You will probably never run out of content unless you truly dedicate yourself to studying this game.

So for all the praise, where does it have faults? Well, it does have a high skill floor. I was routinely getting destroyed when I started out. I am personally accustomed to reactive gameplay. I'm the kind of person that will play Smash Bros. with about half the items enabled and stage events enabled, embracing the need to react to random events. So when this game is destroying [b]me[/b], I feel this game will basically shut out a lot of players who can't deal with its seemingly chaotic nature with so many things to consider at a fast pace. Thankfully the Bard exists for those players to let them play at their own pace, but that is not readily obvious, and if you need to remove the rhythm element to enjoy this, you're losing out on basically all the other characters. The game is also dependent on you enjoying chiptune and a pixelated visual style (although thankfully the game does make it obvious that you can use your own music). I think it could benefit from the ability reskin to a smoother art style / soundtrack, even if I personally am fine with its presentation as-is.

So all together, the main elements that will draw people in to liking this seem to be:
* Brutal but fair challenge
* Tactical decision-making on a fast pace
* Standard roguelike exploration
* Retro art & music

Fortunately for me, I am all-in on all of this, but I can see how this would not work for some players. Also, I was encouraged to try this from the late great TotalBiscuit, RIP.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is one of the most engaging, fun, and in-the-zone games that exists.

The point of the game is to be extremely rhythmic, as you can obviously see. Everything happens to the beat. Everything. All the movement, all the animation, EVERYTHING. Everything moves on a predictable pattern, and everything is telegraphed really well so that you know what’s happening, when it’s happening, and what the consequences and benefits of that thing happening are. Since everything happens on the beat, you’re trapped in the beat and are always thinking a beat ahead. At the core, the game is basically turn based, but it’s the opposite of unengaging because you have to constantly move and think on the beat.

The music is essential to the experience though, and if it sucked, the game would. Fortunately, the music is insanely good, and extremely clear on when the beat is, without intruding on the music itself. It makes you move along to the beat in real life, so you know it does its job better than well for its in-game purpose. Also, in my opinion, Necrodancer has one of, if not the best, soundtracks to listen to by itself.

The story connection to gameplay is as close as it could possibly be. You’re trapped in the beat, having to constantly move and think on your feet. The story is the same, Cadence is trapped in the beat, needing to kill the Necrodancer to break free and get the lute. When you finally do kill the Necrodancer, the run is over instantly, and you break free as the player, and also in the story. This is the most technically engaging story to probably ever exist.

Whenever you beat that boss, or that all-zones run… when the run is over because you won, you did it… it is probably my favorite feeling ever. Once the run is over you realize you’ve been vibrating, almost parailyzed, and it is in my opinion the most satisfying feeling in the world.

You did it, you’re free of the beat… you accomplished something you didn’t think you had the skill, mastery, determination, perseverance, and rhythm to do so.

Necrodancer perfected this genre with its first try.

[h1][u][b]Introduction[/b][/u][/h1]

The Crypt of the NecroDancer is a very unique addition to the genre of rogue-like games. Never before a game like this has been seen in the gaming industry which combines the elements of a dungeon crawler and rhythm-based gameplay that is produced with such quality and immersiveness.

[h1][u][b]Gameplay[/b][/u][/h1]

In this game, you are forced to move to the beat of the soundtracks (except for one character) where the tempo of each beat is shown by the meter on the bottom part of the screen and will vary depending on the track being played. 

Violating this rule will reduce your multiplier to the lowest set value (though the permanent upgrade addition will still persist), and is also the same if you were to take damage. Players are able to build this up by landing successful hits to an enemy and is kept level by staying on the beat.

After every session on any mode (either by clearing the zone or by dying), the items and coins you gained will be removed and reset back to your default equipment except for "diamonds", which is used for certain upgrades/locks/unlocks to various NPCs in the game lobby.  

The game modes are basically divided into two, separate zones and all-zones mode. The only difference with either mode is that the upgrades that you have bought are only present on separate zones and that the player is required to play through zone 1 to 4 on all-zones mode for it to be cleared.

[h1][u][b]The Pros[/b][/u][/h1]

[list]

[*][b]Excellent Audio[/b] - As a rhythm game, the audio should be flawless and on-spot to the theme as it is the genre's main attribute, and this is a perfect example to it. The soundtracks may vary depending on the stage the player is in or by the character they are using (which are remixed tracks of the original version, for example, playing as Aria will play the metal version of the tracks).

[*][b]Large Array of Playable Characters and Game Modes[/b] - This standard element of every session-based game is also present, in which it gives longevity and versatility to the game play. These new characters can be unlocked by clearing zones, and each and everyone of them have their own perks as well as rules and restrictions (aside from the default unlocked characters) to follow. Violating these rules will result in immediate death if you don't have an item that could save you.   

[*][b]High Replay Value[/b] - A sign of a great game is that it will always have you longing for another round even if you failed miserably or even rage-quitted. May it be from the satisfaction of clearing a difficult zone or unlocking achievements or revisiting your favorite tracks, a game with a high replay value makes the money you spent on it worthwhile.

[*][b]Steam Integration[/b] - From the very helpful Steam Cloud feature up to the Steamworks' additional mods that you can add, this is great for those people who wants to spice the game up more and modify it to match their taste.

[/list]

[h1][u][b]The Cons[/b][/u][/h1]

[list]

[*][b]Repetitive Audio[/b] - Given the nature of rogue-likes, you will die and restart the levels more than you would like to and this means that you will be forced the hear the soundtracks of each floor again and again. Supposedly, this is only minus if the soundtracks of the game are bad (which is not the case in here), but still I would like to cover all bases for those who are interested in buying the game.

[*][b]Immense Difficulty Levels[/b] - By no means that this is a BAD thing, BUT if you are a casual player who enjoys more of a relaxing game play or just aren't good at playing the game or has bad body coordination, then this game MIGHT not be for you (though it doesn't mean that you shouldn't give it a try). Honestly, I am bad at this game that I could only clear levels with Bard (which is easy-mode) and barely with the other characters.

[/list]

[h1][u][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/u][/h1]

This game is the fruit of undeniable passion and love of the developers, and indeed is a masterpiece of its own genre to be said at the very least. Also, if you are a fan of games with great soundtracks, you won't make a mistake buying this!

If this game was just a roguelike with a rhythm twist, I wouldn't have played this game for 400 something hours. I mean, yes, it is; that's what it set out to do, and managed to zone in on exactly what was fun about the idea with surgical precision. Mix that with some really rocking soundtrack and lots of highly diverse content... is it any wonder this game blew up like it did?

Okay, okay. Those are some strong words that don't really say anything, you probably think. I'll try to explain, but the best way to summarise is this: not only you need to move and attack in a very specific rhythm, you also need to be on the lookout for your enemies and predict what they'll do, so you can exploit holes in their patterns. And having to do both at the same time makes your brain work at like 400% efficiency; And that insane level of engagement is this sweet syrup that is the very base of what makes Necrodancer so freaking fun.

[h1]Highly diverse content[/h1]
Let's talk about weapons. By default, you've got the dagger - it can deal 1 damage to an adjacent enemy. Typical, if you're familiar with the classic roguelike design. But then you get the spear; it can hit an enemy that's one field away from you, or right next to you. Or a longsword? It can hit them both in one swing. Or my personal fav, a rapier: it can hit an adjacent enemy, but if you attack an enemy that's one space away, you will lunge towards them and deal double damage. Risky, but rewarding.

There's a lot more weapons, and many are much more exotic and difficult to use; the point I'm making is that your options will vary greatly depending on what gear you have. Keep in mind, this is all in addition to having to move to the rhythm, and the enemies still do the same patterns! Getting the picture yet?

[h1]They lead, you follow[/h1]
I could tell you more about different kinds of gear (there's a lot), but let's talk about enemies instead. The base game (without DLC) is split into 4 zones. Each of them has mostly unique enemies, and they don't just scale up in damage/health; all of them have different patterns and mechanics. At first the patterns are easy and there are no secondary effects, and most enemies move slower than you. But then armoured enemies show up, requiring you to either bypass of break through their shields (not always possible). Then you get enemies that phase through walls. Then you get enemies which run away when you face them, and close in on you when you turn your back to them. Then you get enemies that will parry all your attacks and counterattack, forcing you to do a counter-counter. And so on. That's just a small sample, by the way.

To add yet another shelf to this trove of content, let me mention... the characters. Yeah, there are many unlockable characters, and almost all of them have some kind of quirk that completely switches up the gameplay. There's a guy who can only use bombs, but they're infinite and he can kick them. There's a guy that dies when picking up gold. There's a chick that can't attack at all, but she can confuse enemies. They're usually harder to play than Cadence, the main heroine. Two of those characters warrant a mention: Melody and Aria.

[h1]Dancing queens, feat. DJ DannyB[/h1]
See, if you want to beat the story of the game, you have to first win as Cadence, which unlocks Melody - and she in turn unlocks Aria on victory. Melody is generally similar to Cadence, except her health is a little lower and she's got a unique weapon which can't be switched out. Aria on the other hand is a completely different story. She dies in one hit, can only use the dagger, and dies if you miss a beat. It's a gigantic difficulty spike; I don't know how I managed to beat Aria's episode, I just know it took me forever and I couldn't replicate that feat since. Still, beating her is only required to see the ending, but it doesn't really change anything - you still have access to everything else.

All three heroines have their own unique mixes of the soundtrack - and there's a lot of additional mixes, so you can switch things around quite often. Every stage has its own track, and they slowly increase in BPM the further you get. That probably goes without saying, but the music is full of bangers; It's composed by Danny Baranowsky - you zoomers probably don't know who that is, but he was the composer for early indie darlings: Super Meat Boy and original Binding of Isaac. Quality ensured!

[h1]Party until dawn[/h1]
I've been doing daily challenges for years now, it's part of my evening routine. After all this time, if I had to complain about something... it's that certain builds are just clearly superior to others, so most of my runs end up looking exactly the same towards the end. I deal with this with some self-imposed rules, f.ex. first weapon I pick up is my weapon for the entire run. Or I use only exotic weapons which are hard to use. It's not a necessity, though; the game's still fun, even after all those years.

As a closing statement, I'd like to point towards a certain other game by this developer: Cadence of Hyrule. It's a Zelda game with Necrodancer twist. Let me rephrase that: Nintendo, who's famously super defensive of their IP, granted a Zelda license to an indie studio. If that's not a reliable mark of quality then I don't know what is. Coincidentally, I believe Necrodancer to be much better of the two; so what are you waiting for? Get down on that dance floor! Even for a full price, this game will always be worth it. Enjoy!

I waited way too long to pick this one up. On one hand, I love rhythm games and was huge into Rock Band's drums back in the day. On the other hand, roguelikes are a bit overdone at this point and even a game with a huge amount of depth can be a turnoff when you play for 30 hours and only see less than 10% of the content, often because RNGesus hates you.

I'm going to assume that you enjoy rhythm games if you're considering this one, Crypt of the NecroDancer does three things that roguelikes in general can learn from.

The first is that everything is predictable, even when it's random. The majority of enemies follow a strict algorithmic pattern and the better you are at discerning these patterns and reacting to them quickly, the better you will do. Red Bats' random movements are countered by paying attention to what tiles they are on and what tiles you're on. Bosses have reliable strategies that allow them to be taken out with zero damage suffered, even the ones like Death Metal who have aspects of randomness included. Item drops are random, but this matters less as you unlock higher and higher difficulties that are designed to deprive you of gear and demand perfection.

The second thing is that the majority of things are unlocked within a relatively short span of play for a roguelike, about 10 hours. Furthermore, competitive modes such as the Daily Challenge and All Zones/Seeded put everyone on a completely level playing field from the start. No system of unlocks that favors 300+ hour players over the new installs, which is frankly a very good thing. It's not just even popular roguelikes, competitive has become a joke across a wide array of genres due to the industry's addiction to progression systems. It's used as an artificial longevity tactic and even though the store page isn't all 100+ hour reviewers, you know those reviewers' time wasn't wasted by grinding either. This trait gives Crypt of the Necrodancer more of an arcade feel, which is appropriate as all zone runs generally last under an hour. (with the world record seeded speedrun being under 2 minutes)

The last kudos goes to the fact that you can enable an option (off by default) to make item names/descriptions visible. I love this feature -- a certain other mega-popular roguelike lacks this feature and as a result it feels like a Mediawiki simulator, constantly disrupting the flow of play. There are a few items without descriptions but these are clearly cursed or "double-edged sword" type items, so that's fine.

Although not tagged as such, it's worth mentioning that this game is very difficult. You have a lot more information to process than other rhythm games, especially as enemies start becoming more numerous. The difficulty spikes drastically once you unlock the final story mode character, who can only survive two hits or missed beats. Needless to say the YouTube rendition of all the cutscenes is very popular as a result, but just looking at the global achievement stats (and the lack of achievers) will tell you that this game isn't messing around. This isn't a huge problem due to customization options being robust enough to suit any difficulty level, though the one thing they got wrong was hiding the "double time" character behind the "gold one-shots you" character. It's probably justifiable by difficulty scaling, but it's not all that justifiable by locking what many would consider to be the "fun hard" character behind "tedious hard" one. But this is a small nitpick honestly.

There are plenty of ways to customize the game. The options menu supports a wide range of preferences, always important for letting people feel "in the zone" in a rhythm game. There's a modding system, though I haven't used it much yet. The song importer is pretty good, and it accurately timed songs that I ripped from my CD's as WMA and then turned into OGG with Audacity. (only mp3 and ogg are supported) Digital purchases will probably fare just as well. PC rips will require manual timing, which works well enough. It also gives you options to play songs at half or double time, which you might want with higher BPM genres like Metal. Necrodancer seems to have a range for where BPM should be, and halves any that exceed that range -- so you'll want to either play your Dragonforce CD as Bolt, or manually set it to 2x speed.

One final positive to mention, and also advice for new players -- it's playable with a dance pad, but you probably need to be superhuman to have a chance in the more difficult modes. Keyboard is also supported, and if you're playing on keyboard, remap the spell/item/misc keys right away and disable the default combos. This seems to make the input more responsive...or maybe I expected it to and it just seems more responsive. It's also good to get used to your own layout right away as the inprecision of two key input will eventually end up biting you the more the game demands perfection.

All in all, this is an amazing game...and I'll be there on day 1 if an expansion or sequel comes out.

[*]The game doesn't feel like it's in Early Access. Aside from the couple of features not yet programmed in, such as the full selection of characters to play as, everything is as polished as you'd hope the finished game would be.

[*]Despite dying more times than I care to count, I have yet to feel frustrated with the game. And I can get quite easily frustrated with games that kill me a lot. But with NecroDancer, I'm only ever frustrated with myself, for not quite moving fast enough, or panicking at a crucial moment. In a world of unfair gaming experiences, Crypt of the NecroDancer is a beacon of light that invites to you blame yourself, rather than the game!

[*]Yes, the game is challenging. Despite having played it long enough to know the attack patterns of most monsters in the game, the monsters frequently - shockingly often, in fact - get the better of me. It's not just a matter of learning the game. Thanks to the fast-paced rhythm aspect, it's instead a matter of calling upon your knowledge at a moment's notice, and staying calm even at the sight of a minotaur charging towards you, or a red dragon preparing to unleash fiery chaos upon you in the next half a second.

[*]The soundtrack is one of the best I've ever heard in a game.

There is simply nothing to criticise - at least, nothing apart from the most minor issues, such as monsters occasionally getting in each other's ways and forcing each other to remain stationary until you kill them. But that rarely happens, and it's certainly nothing even close to a game-breaking issue - it's just a quirk of the game. And seeing as it's still in Early Access, I'm surprised that's the only one I can think of!

Closing remarks: Crypt of the NecroDancer is amazing. One of the most flawless games I've ever played. If it appeals to you then buy it. You will not be disappointed, I guarantee it.

Indie Rogue-Likes are a dime a dozen on Steam these days, but Necrodancer stands out by being both creative and really, really fun to play.

While it may not be the next Nuclear Throne in terms of depth, Necrodancer does have a few tricks up its sleeves to keep things interesting. A half dozen or so unlockable characters (all with their own unique twists and stipulations), a customizable item pool, and of course the traditional random level generation are here, but I often found the smaller things, like being able to dig through walls, more fun to mess around with. There's a lot of replay value as well, if you don't mind the challenge that is.

And speaking of challenge, it can be a surprisingly difficult game at times. Although there's just 4 levels (with 3 stages each), you'll know the ins and outs of every one of them before long because of how much experimenting the game wants you to do. Stuck on a level? Try using a new item, or looking for a specific room.

But let's be real here. The soundtrack is an incredibly crucial part of any good rhythm game, and Necrodancer knocks its music out of the park. This isn't a game OST pretending to be a dance album, it IS a dance album. Hands down.

Everyone involved in this project has poured their heart and soul into it, and it really shows. If you wanna try a rhythm game, you absolutely have to go with this one.

This game has what every other rhythm game was lacking for me, decisions and thought. In other rhythm games whatever you do doesn't need planning or thought but memorization and repetition. Sure, the gratification you get from completing more conventional rhythm games can be good, but in this game as you were the one in control the whole time and not a mapmaker, you feel so satisfied by the end of a run (or unsatisfied if you need to git gud).

The music is simply superb for all characters, both the themes of each level and boss fit their places very well. You can listen to any part of the songs almost (Aria...) indefinitely. Some remixes do make it hard to feel the rhythm at times but you can select a different remix or the og themes to combat that or simply get better ears. 

The game controls are great and easy to learn aside from a few combos maybe, but you can set those to their own keys if you want to.

The enemies can feel repetitive within each level as there aren't many of them, but their myriad of interactions with the map, other enemies and the traps will make up for that for sure. So many times I was amazed at seeing an interaction I simply did not think possible. Boss and miniboss variety is also a bit of an issue I feel, but I understand it's tough to design unique bosses for a game like this, and it's really not the main part of the game aside from the end bosses. You're mostly playing to clear the floors and beat the end boss. 

There are plenty of items and modifiers within the game that you really have to think about. Would you like to see where all the enemies are in the floor? Well you can, but they will return the favor. Would you like extra strength at the cost of being able to discern the enemies well? These choices come up every run and you have to choose well to win.

The characters have fascinating playstyles that can be tough to get accustomed to or plain tough. What I can guarantee is that they are all fun in their own ways. You want to learn the movements of the enemies better and plan more? There's the Bard for you. A simple run? Cadence will do great. You want to torture yourself? You have pleeeeenty of options.

Overall, this is one of my favorite games ever and I can't see many aspects of it I dislike/find lacking. I give it a 9.5/10

[I]Crypt of the NecroDancer[/I] only got my attention when its spin-off/crossover, [I]Cadence of Hyrule[/I], was released on the Nintendo Switch. Intrigued by its fascinating game mechanics, I decided to give [I]CotND[/I] a try despite it not featuring characters or music from the beloved [I]Zelda[/I] franchise.

[I]CotND[/I] is a challenging game, but it’s fun. It’s especially so if you enjoy music and rhythm games. The fact that it’s a roguelike means that each playthrough will be different, and you can’t just memorize your way through each crypt. Admittedly, seeing the same crypt backgrounds through repeated playing (mostly from dying frequently) can still get tiresome with time.

For those who are unfamiliar with roguelikes, such as I, playing a challenging one like [I]CotND[/I] can be frustrating at first. What made the game even more annoying for me, not only as a newcomer to the genre, but also a person who often needs to quit playing games at a drop of a dime, was that I couldn’t save my game mid-level. However, I soon got over these “annoyances”, and started to enjoy whatever [I]CotND[/I] delivers in the variable amount of time I had to play it.

Honestly, the more you play, the better feel you’ll have of the game’s – no pun intended – rhythm. And in no time, you’ll rack up more diamonds to purchase better equipment and consumables to level up your character. If you’re patient and skilled enough, you’ll unlock and move on to the next zone purely through your proficiency. There is no slacking or cheating your way through [I]CotND[/I] – every reward, unlockable and achievement has to be earned.

[I]CotND[/I] is not going to be a game I’ll ever finish, mainly because I don’t have the time to play it regularly to refine my skills. But that’s okay, because I recognize that although [I]CotND[/I] may not be the ideal game for me, it’s still a gem. Just like how no two live concert performances are alike, every game you play of [I]CotND[/I] will feel different, fresh and challenging. This is a unique, innovative game that’s worth trying, and worthy of attention because its originality can be easily overlooked in the sea of headlines-grabbing AAA game titles.
